records.our_prose: Chard is a biennial and, unlike spinach and lettuce, does not bolt from summer heat or long days; it flowers only after it has lived through a winter, so a spring planting crops cleanly into fall without running to seed. The two ways to trigger premature bolting in the first year are sowing too early into cold soil, which can vernalize the young plants, and an unusually cold spring snap; avoid both by sowing once the soil has warmed past about 50°F. Overwintered plants will bolt as spring warms, so crop them before the stalk elongates and start a fresh sowing.

records.our_prose: Swiss chard (Beta vulgaris) is a leafy member of the goosefoot family grown for its large, tender leaves and its broad, often vividly colored edible stalks. It is the same species as the beet, selected for leaf and stem rather than root, and it shares the beet's pests, diseases, and multigerm seedball. Its defining trait is an unusual tolerance of both heat and cold: unlike lettuce and spinach, chard does not bolt in summer heat or long days (as a biennial it flowers only after a winter), so a single spring planting crops straight through the summer and well into fall, and in mild zones it overwinters for a harvest that spans much of the year. Harvested cut-and-come-again, the outer leaves picked while the crown keeps producing, one chard plant yields for months. The colorful-stemmed types such as Bright Lights are as ornamental as they are useful, and the stalks cook as a vegetable in their own right.

records.our_prose: Aim for a soil pH of about 6.0 to 7.0, slightly acidic to neutral. The University of Minnesota notes chard tolerates soil somewhat more acidic than spinach, as low as about pH 6.0, and Clemson cites a 6.0 to 6.5 range; like the beet it is the same species as, chard also handles mildly alkaline soil (to about 7.5) better than most leafy greens. Acidity well below 6.0 is the main risk, where germination and micronutrient uptake suffer. A standard soil test removes the guesswork before sowing.

records.our_prose: St. George's Dixie belt (Mojave-edge high desert) grows Swiss chard on a single direct-sown spring stand, per Utah State University Extension's suggested vegetable planting dates for Utah, which gives St. George a Group B (Semi-Hardy) date around March 1. Leaves are ready to cut in about 55 days, from late April into early June. USU Extension's Washington County frost and elevation notes put St. George over 100°F in June, July, and August, and chard leaves toughen and turn bitter in that heat, so the stand is cut back and let go before it, and USU's suggested planting dates document no St. George fall chard window, so the bed rests through the hottest months rather than carrying a second stand.
